subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 56-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with vomiting of bright red blood and black, tarry stools. Endoscopy shows bleeding esophageal varices. The bleeding source is located above the ligament of Treitz.
question: Which of the following best classifies this patient's gastrointestinal bleeding?

options.text: Lower GI bleeding from a colonic source, given the bright red blood
Lower GI bleeding because the source is distal to the pylorus
Upper GI bleeding because it originates distal to the ligament of Treitz
Upper GI bleeding because it originates proximal to the ligament of Treitz
Lower GI bleeding from angiodysplasia of the cecum

explanation_correct: Upper GI bleeding is defined as hemorrhage originating proximal to the ligament of Treitz (the suspensory ligament of the duodenum). It typically presents with hematemesis and/or melena and is associated with peptic ulcer disease and variceal hemorrhage. This patient's esophageal varices in cirrhosis are a classic upper GI source. The anatomic dividing line, not the color of the blood, determines the classification.

explanation_incorrect.A: Bright red blood can appear with brisk upper bleeding; the location above the ligament of Treitz makes this upper, not lower, GI bleeding.
explanation_incorrect.B: The pylorus is not the dividing line; the ligament of Treitz is the anatomic boundary between upper and lower GI bleeding.
explanation_incorrect.C: Bleeding distal to the ligament of Treitz would be classified as lower GI bleeding, the opposite of this case.
explanation_incorrect.E: Angiodysplasia is a lower GI cause and would not explain hematemesis or esophageal varices in cirrhosis.

educationalObjective: Upper GI bleeding arises proximal to the ligament of Treitz and presents with hematemesis and/or melena, as with varices or PUD.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 72-year-old man notices painless bright red blood mixed with stool over the past day. He has a history of constipation and no hematemesis or melena. The bleeding source is presumed to be distal to the ligament of Treitz.
question: Which of the following best characterizes this patient's bleeding?

options.text: Lower GI bleeding distal to the ligament of Treitz, commonly from diverticulosis
Upper GI bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz from a duodenal ulcer
Upper GI bleeding from esophageal varices
Lower GI bleeding from a gastric ulcer on the lesser curvature
Upper GI bleeding presenting as hematochezia from Zollinger-Ellison syndrome

explanation_correct: Lower GI bleeding originates distal to the ligament of Treitz and usually presents with hematochezia (bright red blood per rectum). Causes include inflammatory bowel disease, diverticulosis, angiodysplasia, hemorrhoids, anal fissure, and cancer. In an older adult with painless bright red blood, diverticulosis is a classic cause. The absence of hematemesis/melena and a source distal to the ligament of Treitz make this lower GI bleeding.

explanation_incorrect.B: A duodenal ulcer is an upper GI source proximal to the ligament of Treitz and typically causes hematemesis or melena, not painless hematochezia.
explanation_incorrect.C: Esophageal varices are an upper GI source that would present with hematemesis and melena, especially in cirrhosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: A gastric ulcer on the lesser curvature is an upper GI source that may bleed from the left gastric artery but would not cause isolated hematochezia.
explanation_incorrect.E: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome causes upper GI duodenal ulcers from gastrin excess, not lower GI bleeding or isolated hematochezia.

educationalObjective: Painless hematochezia from a source distal to the ligament of Treitz is lower GI bleeding, classically from diverticulosis in older adults.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 60-year-old woman with a history of alcohol use presents with weakness and black, tarry, foul-smelling stools. She has no visible bright red blood. Her hemoglobin is 8 g/dL.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's stool findings?

options.text: Lower GI bleeding from angiodysplasia, because melena localizes to the colon
Lower GI bleeding from hemorrhoids, which commonly cause black stools
Upper GI bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz, as with peptic ulcer disease or varices
Lower GI bleeding from an anal fissure with slow oozing
Upper GI bleeding from diverticulosis of the sigmoid colon

explanation_correct: Melena, black tarry foul-smelling stool, indicates upper GI bleeding with blood that has been digested during transit. Upper GI bleeding originates proximal to the ligament of Treitz and is associated with peptic ulcer disease and variceal hemorrhage. In a patient with alcohol use, esophageal varices are a strong consideration. The key teaching point is that melena points to an upper source even when no hematemesis is reported.

explanation_incorrect.A: Angiodysplasia is a lower GI cause that typically produces painless hematochezia or occult bleeding, not melena.
explanation_incorrect.B: Hemorrhoids are a lower GI source that cause bright red blood, not black tarry stools.
explanation_incorrect.D: An anal fissure causes bright red blood with pain, not melena, and is distal to the ligament of Treitz.
explanation_incorrect.E: Diverticulosis is a lower GI source distal to the ligament of Treitz and would not produce melena.

educationalObjective: Melena signifies upper GI bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz, most often from PUD or varices.
source: Generated from 9. Gastrointestinal.pdf - Pathology: Upper and lower gastrointestinal bleeding

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 34-year-old woman has intermittent bright red blood per rectum with no hematemesis. Bleeding is confirmed to arise distal to the ligament of Treitz.
question: Which of the following is a recognized cause of this type of bleeding?

options.text: Esophageal varices
Gastric antral ulcer
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome
Mallory-Weiss tear at the gastroesophageal junction
Angiodysplasia

explanation_correct: Lower GI bleeding originates distal to the ligament of Treitz and is associated with inflammatory bowel disease, diverticulosis, angiodysplasia, hemorrhoids, anal fissure, and cancer. Angiodysplasia is a vascular malformation, classically of the cecum or right colon in older adults, that causes painless hematochezia. The other listed conditions are upper GI sources proximal to the ligament of Treitz.

explanation_incorrect.A: Esophageal varices are an upper GI source that presents with hematemesis and melena in portal hypertension.
explanation_incorrect.B: A gastric antral ulcer is a peptic ulcer proximal to the ligament of Treitz and would cause upper GI bleeding.
explanation_incorrect.C: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome produces upper GI duodenal ulcers from gastrin excess, not lower GI bleeding.
explanation_incorrect.D: A Mallory-Weiss tear is a mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction and is an upper GI source after retching.

educationalObjective: Angiodysplasia is a classic lower GI bleeding source distal to the ligament of Treitz.
